title: Interest rates: Traders eye fourth rate rise after jobs surge
full_text:
Bond traders are all but certain that the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise interest rates for a fourth time this year after June employment figures smashed expectations on Thursday.
Markets were swift to react to the 76,300 jump in employment numbers last month against the consensus expected 15,000 increase. The May number was also revised up to 44,000 workers, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.4 per cent.
Traders are now pricing in a 36 per cent chance of higher borrowing costs when the RBA meets next month and are now fully priced for one more increase by year-end that would take the cash rate to 4.6 per cent - which would be the highest since 2011.
Before the employment data was published, markets had priced in a 22 per cent chance next month and 79 per cent by Christmas.
The RBA has raised interest rates three times in quick succession this year to try and get ahead of an unexpected acceleration in inflation that has been further exacerbated by the outbreak of the Iran war.
Economists say much depends on next week's quarterly inflation numbers. If the trimmed mean inflation - the central bank's preferred measure - comes in above expectations at 1 per cent it could seal the deal for a fourth rate increase.
"The strong employment numbers make a hike more likely. But the key for the RBA and the market will be the CPI," said Challenger chief economist Jonathan Kearns. "My view is that the market has been under-pricing the chance of a hike, I think it's a 50-50 call."
In currency markets, the Australian dollar rose as much as 0.3 per cent on Thursday, above US70¢, and the yield on policy-sensitive three-year government notes climbed as much as five basis points as traders ramped up their rate rise bets.
Barrenjoey chief rates strategist Andrew Lilley also said much depended on next week's inflation numbers. He, too, said the RBA would have no choice but to raise rates in August if the trimmed mean came in at 1 per cent, which would be higher than Barrenjoey's forecast of 0.9 per cent.
Kearns said an inflation print of 0.9 per cent or higher would be enough to force more tightening.
"We've had high inflation for most of the almost four years and the risk is that inflation expectations creep up," Kearns, who is a former RBA executive, added. "The RBA needs policy tight enough for the market to credibly believe inflation is heading back to target."
The other factor, according to Lilley, is the oil price, which has been pushing back towards $US100 per barrel.
Brent crude rose 2.6 per cent on Thursday to trade near $US96 amid further unrest in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants said they attacked two Saudi Arabian tankers in the Red Sea, escalating the conflict and threatening deeper supply disruptions.
"The big question is how long the spike in oil prices lasts for," said Lilley. "If it goes back toward $US100 and stays there until the meeting, then we'd be concerned around second round effects again in a way that the RBA weren't in the June meeting."
